title: The Hard Problem
objective: After this level you can explain David Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness and how it differs from the easy problems of explaining brain functions.
summary: Chalmers separated the easy problems of explaining brain functions from the hard problem of why they come with experience; the Churchlands replied that neuroscience makes the gap hard to imagine.

cards.headline: Explain everything your brain does. Is something still left over?
cards.body: In 1995 David Chalmers split the puzzle of consciousness into many easy problems and one hard one.

cards.headline: The “easy” problems
cards.body: Chalmers’s easy problems include explaining how we tell stimuli apart and react to them, pull information together, report our mental states, focus attention, control behavior, and differ between waking and sleep. Easy is relative, he admitted: they may take a century or two of hard empirical work. But cognitive science and neuroscience know how to attack them.

cards.headline: The hard one
cards.body: The hard problem is experience itself. When your brain processes colors and sounds, there is also something it is like: the quality of deep blue, the sensation of middle C. Why should all that information processing come with an inner life at all? That, for Chalmers, is the hard problem.

cards.headline: Why functions don’t settle it
cards.body: Remember Level 34, where mental states were defined by their jobs? Chalmers argued that the hard problem isn’t about performing functions at all. Explain every function the brain performs, and the question remains: why is the performance accompanied by experience? The standard methods for explaining functions leave it standing.

cards.headline: The Churchlands push back
cards.body: Not everyone accepts the split. Paul and Patricia Churchland replied that the more you learn about how the brain produces experience, the harder it becomes to imagine creatures with brain processes like ours but no consciousness. Learn more about the brain, they argue, and the gap gets harder even to picture.

cards.headline: The Hard Problem: the big picture
learned: Hard problem: why any of it is experienced
Churchlands: brain science makes the gap hard to picture

questions.prompt: Match each item with the kind of problem Chalmers says it is.
questions.explanation: Focusing attention and reporting mental states are easy problems. The quality of deep blue and the sensation of middle C belong to the hard problem: experience itself.

questions.prompt: How does the hard problem differ from the easy problems, according to Chalmers?

options.label: Easy: how functions work; hard: why they come with experience
Easy ones are about animals, the hard one about people
The hard one needs bigger computers
options.rationale: More computing power only helps with functions.

options.label: Easy ones are already fully solved
options.rationale: He said they may take a century or two.

questions.explanation: The easy problems are about explaining functions; the hard problem is why performing them is accompanied by experience.

questions.prompt: Functionalism defines mental states by their roles. Why does Chalmers think explaining those roles leaves the hard problem standing?

options.label: Because roles can’t be explained at all
options.rationale: He called explaining functions the easy part.

options.label: Because the hard problem isn’t about performing functions
Because functionalism turns out to be a form of dualism after all
Because only octopuses have roles
options.rationale: The roles apply to humans too.

questions.explanation: Chalmers argued that even with every function explained, the question of why it comes with experience remains.
